name: Dialogue Engines and Virtual Docents
title: Dialogue Engines and Virtual Docents
answer: Dialogue engines and virtual docents are interactive artworks that use conversational AI to act as guides, narrators, or interlocutors in galleries, museums, and public spaces. They range from screen-based avatars that answer visitor questions about an exhibition to ambient voice installations that respond to movement or spoken prompts. The work sits at the intersection of performance, curation, and human-computer interaction, treating the exchange itself as the artistic material. Unlike a kiosk or help desk, these systems are designed to shape attention, provoke reflection, or create a sense of presence rather than simply deliver information.

Unlike a kiosk or help desk, these systems are designed to shape attention, provoke reflection, or create a sense of presence rather than simply deliver information.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These works typically run on a combination of cloud-hosted large language models, local speech recognition, and text-to-speech services, often coordinated by a small control application on a museum computer or embedded device. Many installations use a microphone array and speaker system tuned for noisy gallery floors, with a fallback to typed input on a tablet or phone when voice recognition is unreliable. Some artists run smaller open-weight models on a local GPU to avoid network latency or to keep visitor audio from leaving the building. The site's live model counts for image, video, and audio generation are not directly relevant here, but the same underlying transformer architectures are often adapted for dialogue.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is usually made by writing a system prompt or persona, curating a knowledge base of exhibition facts or poetic fragments, and then rehearsing the model's responses against sample visitor questions. Artists often add rules for turn-taking, silence, interruption, and emotional tone, so the docent does not simply answer but also withholds, redirects, or asks questions back. Some pieces use retrieval-augmented generation over a small set of artist-approved texts to keep answers grounded, while others deliberately allow hallucination as part of the aesthetic. The final tuning is done through live testing with real visitors, adjusting the prompt and audio cues until the interaction feels intentional.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on visitor privacy, consent, and the provenance of the voice and language. Recorded or transcribed visitor speech may be personal data, so many institutions require clear signage, local processing, or short retention periods. The voice used by a virtual docent may be licensed from an actor or synthesized from a living or deceased person's recordings, raising questions of permission and likeness. Copyright in the model's outputs is unsettled, and an artwork that quotes or paraphrases exhibition texts, poems, or historical letters can create disputes over attribution. Provenance documentation should record which model, prompt, knowledge sources, and voice were used, so the piece can be preserved or restaged later.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: These systems are moving toward longer, more embodied interactions, with docents that remember a visitor across a visit or across multiple rooms and respond to gaze, gesture, and movement as well as speech. Smaller, faster models are making it practical to run a full dialogue engine on a phone or a single board computer inside a sculpture, reducing reliance on cloud APIs. Artists are also exploring docents that speak in multiple languages, switch between historical and contemporary registers, or collaborate with human guides in real time. The main open question is whether these systems can sustain a genuine artistic exchange rather than a scripted Q&A, and how institutions will credit and maintain them as living works.
